title: How I make films in New York on an indie budget.
dek: Jugaad, a phone full of friends, and a city that works as a free set.
short: Films in New York on an indie budget

cover.alt: Still from The Last Pizza, a survival thriller written, directed and edited by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil, with Nathan Flores, Chris and Yi Chan: the delivery guy alone on a New York rooftop at dusk
cover.cap: [The Last Pizza](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3YfriOGVA4w): a thriller shot on New York rooftops for $50.

body: I did the one-year filmmaking conservatory at the [New York Film Academy](https://www.nyfa.edu/), focused on directing. We did everything: directing, cinematography, writing, acting. Classes ran five or six days a week, and weekends were for shooting.

I figured out fast that I couldn't spend on my films what a lot of my classmates spent on theirs. I come from a middle-class family in India. So I did what we do back home: jugaad. Find the smart, cheap way to get it done.

I made friends everywhere. Actors, musical theatre students, cinematographers, anyone in the building. I went to events and filmmaking meetups and talked about my stories with whoever would listen. So when I had a film to make, I already knew who was right for it. I called them, and because they were friends who trusted the project, they came on as collaborators.

Call your friends and family first. You don't have to hire every role off [Backstage](https://www.backstage.com/) or pay for an AD and a DP on day one. Your friends might be better, and every shoot turns them into a team that's there for the next one.

You can see it in my credits. Nathan Flores is in [The Last Pizza](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3YfriOGVA4w), [Agent X](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GSIja5IH9eo) and [Before We Leave](https://youtu.be/vTM1-v4kuSQ). Yi Chan (Ethan) acted in The Last Pizza, shot Before We Leave and was my AD on Agent X. Cito shot The Last Pizza and ran sound on Agent X. Same family, different films.

body.alt: Title card for Before We Leave, a Chekhovian short directed by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil at the New York Film Academy: Giulia Mate looks down on a park bench as Nathan Flores watches her, under the words Too late?
body.cap: [Before We Leave](https://youtu.be/vTM1-v4kuSQ): one day, a skeleton crew, no budget. Giulia Mate and Nathan Flores, shot by Yi Chan (Ethan).

body.alt: Still from Agent X, an interrogation scene directed by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil: Dillon Cain as the agent leans across the table toward Nathan Flores as the prisoner
body.cap: [Agent X](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GSIja5IH9eo): Dillon Cain and Nathan Flores, with Yi Chan (Ethan) as AD and Cito on sound.

body: Today, if you asked me for a crew, I could put one together in seconds: DP, AD, actors, sound, a colorist, an editor. That's the whole trick. It's harder if you're shy, I get it. Do it anyway.
Micro dramas: the same family, a bigger slate

The same approach carried into the micro dramas I direct for [Canvas](https://creatorsarethenewstudios.com): 12+ series so far, including [Face Value](/series/face-value/), [Red Flags](/series/red-flags/), [Dear NYC](/series/dear-nyc/), [Taser Fight Championship](/series/taser-fight-championship/) and [Demo Day](/series/demo-day/). Each runs four to ten episodes, every episode under two minutes. The constant on every one: me directing and Abhinav Singla on production.

Around us, the same people keep coming back. Nishita was my AD on Dear NYC. Navya did art on Dear NYC and Red Flags. Karun shot Dear NYC, and Kais Vasaya shot most of the others, including Face Value and Demo Day. Onil Shah colored most of them and shot some too.

body.alt: Dear NYC, a Canvas romance with Ruhani Sharma, written and directed by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil: lifting the mask on a subway platform
body.cap: [Dear NYC](/series/dear-nyc/), with Ruhani Sharma: shot in a day across Manhattan, the subway and the Brooklyn Bridge. AD Nishita, art Navya, DOP Karun.

body.alt: Red Flags, a Canvas romance series with creator Robert Maxwell, directed by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil: a look across the subway car
body.cap: [Red Flags](/series/red-flags/), with creator Robert Maxwell. Art by Navya.

body: Actors I met making short films, like Dillon Cain from Agent X and Cassidy, came back for the micro dramas. Post is friends too. Asla, who edits for my marketing studio, has cut micro drama promos, trailers, teasers and some full episodes. Adarsh has edited with me and Advait has helped. Some of the non-fiction series were edited by friends from my [WLDD](/work/fifteen-people-on-one-floor/) days: Madhur, Karthik and Tushar. And Akhand, my graphic designer from my marketing work, made most of the series posters.
They came from earlier sets, film school, my old office and cold DMs, not from a budget line.

Join every community you can. I'm in New York filmmaker groups on WhatsApp and Facebook, and I meet people on Instagram all the time. When someone's work catches your eye, message them. Don't overthink what they'll think of you. A lot of my DOPs, colorists and editors started as a cold DM on Instagram, and those friends introduced me to more.

My films have cost under $700, and some cost nothing. Locations come from friends too: their apartments become your sets. Outside, New York does a lot of the work. It's backlit almost everywhere you point a camera, and backlight is free production value.

Manhattan streets, the Brooklyn Bridge, Bryant Park, Times Square, Central Park: take a camera and go. I rewrite scenes to fit the places I can get. Subways are easy to shoot, so sometimes the scene just moves to the subway.

On permits: the city's film office says you generally don't need one if you're shooting with a handheld camera or a camera on a tripod, with hand-held gear, and you aren't taking over city property or using vehicles, prop weapons, stunts or actors in police uniforms. [Check the rules](https://www.nyc.gov/site/mome/permits/when-permit-required.page) before you shoot. The subway belongs to the MTA, which has [its own filming rules](https://www.mta.info/doing-business-with-us/filming).
Pick stories your budget can carry

Sci-fi and action eat money. I make realistic films: people talking, drama, comedy, romance, emotions, sometimes close to non-fiction. It's the work I love, and it happens to be the work an indie budget can carry. That's why making indie films came easy to me. It's just who I am as a filmmaker.
None of this is new. Spike Lee shot [She's Gotta Have It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/She%27s_Gotta_Have_It) in Brooklyn in twelve days in the summer of 1985, for $175,000, with a non-union crew.

Over in New Jersey, Kevin Smith made [Clerks](https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/70020/18-black-and-white-facts-about-clerks) for $27,575 in the convenience store where he worked, mostly on maxed-out credit cards. His longtime friend Walt Flanagan played four different customers.

And the micro drama business runs on the same math. A 100-page micro drama script can be shot in about a week, against a month for a feature ([Los Angeles Times](https://www.aol.com/news/hollywoods-romance-micro-dramas-heating-100000961.html)), and whole seasons have been made for $50,000 to $250,000 with affordable, often non-union casts ([Final Draft](https://www.finaldraft.com/blog/what-are-verticals-and-micro-dramas)). Ours are shorter, and we lean even harder on the family.
Be kind to everyone on set, and feed them. Real food, not only pizza. People remember how you treated them, and they'll come back any day you call.
My budget was never money. It was people.

That's the short version. I'll tell the stories behind each shoot in the next few pieces. All my short films are [on the home page](/#films). If you're making something in New York and need a crew, [say hi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nivedkrishna).

title: What happened when we took Canvas to SF and LA Tech Week.
dek: Two events in three days, an Oscar-winning filmmaker on the bill, and the trailers for my series in front of both rooms.
short: Canvas at SF and LA Tech Week

cover.alt: House of 434 founder Shilpi Nayak speaking to guests under string lights at The Hybrid Studio, the Canvas and House of 434 event at LA Tech Week 2026, from the after-movie of the trip by Canvas creative director Nivedkrishna Thavarayil
cover.cap: House of 434 founder Shilpi Nayak at The Hybrid Studio, LA Tech Week, October 12, 2026.

body: In October, Canvas went west for Tech Week: SF Tech Week ran October 5 to 11 and LA Tech Week ran October 12 to 18. I went as Canvas's creative director, with Canvas CEO Abhinav Singla. We hosted two events, went to plenty more, and pitched Canvas at every one.

body: San Francisco: the Canvas launch party

On Saturday, October 10, Anwar Events hosted the [Canvas Launch Party: Creators Are the New Studios](https://luma.com/anwar-8t0d) at 555 Grant Ave. Ilias Anwar moderated a panel with Abhinav, Ben Woollams of TrueRights and Pinto Labs CTO Xavier Santos. [371 guests](https://luma.com/anwar-8t0d) were on the list. Here's [the event post on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/p/DeTXeLNtdPr/).

I played the trailers for the series I directed, and the slate went up in four lanes: fashion, travel, fiction and non-fiction. [The Red Carpet Show](/series/the-red-carpet-show/), our 90-second red carpet interview series with Ilias, was there too.

body: Two days later, on Monday, October 12, House of 434 hosted [The Hybrid Studio: From Oscar-Winning Films to AI-Native Studios](https://luma.com/houseof-nelv) at 11520 W Pico Blvd, listed as an a16z event and in [dot.LA's guide to Monday at LA Tech Week](https://dot.la/la-tech-week-monday-2026-2678063292.html). Shilpi Nayak opened. [Hemal Trivedi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemal_Trivedi), co-founder of ZeroInfinity, presented, and so did Abhinav. Hemal edited Saving Face, the documentary that won the Oscar for Best Documentary Short, and won an Emmy for that edit. Then she and Abhinav sat down for a panel on where craft meets AI, with an investor in the AI video company Higgsfield, and the night closed with an open Q&A.
Around 300 people came. I played our trailers again, and the conversations after were the good kind: filmmakers, AI filmmakers and investors in one room, all asking what a small team can make now.

body: What the week was really for

Hosting was the visible part. The rest of the week, Abhinav and I pitched every day, at every event, to investors, filmmakers and AI filmmakers. In between, we shot about four series across both cities, filming while we hosted and pitched. We also spent a couple of hours talking film with director [Jeremiah S. Chechik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremiah_S._Chechik), who made [National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Lampoon%27s_Christmas_Vacation) and [Benny & Joon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_%26_Joon).

The pitch fits on a hoodie: [creators are the new studios](https://creatorsarethenewstudios.com). Our slate is the proof. [Face Value](/series/face-value/), [Red Flags](/series/red-flags/), [Taser Fight Championship](/series/taser-fight-championship/), [Dear NYC](/series/dear-nyc/) and [Demo Day](/series/demo-day/) are a few of the 12+ series I've directed for Canvas.
[Face Value](/series/face-value/) is already streaming on the Canvas app, with more on the way. If you were in one of those rooms, [say hi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nivedkrishna).

title: I joined WLDD when it was fifteen people on one floor.
dek: From a top floor in Bangalore to owning ScoopWhoop: what a meme agency's early team taught me.

cover.alt: WLDD story by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil: from about 15 people on one floor in Bangalore to about 300 people across Bengaluru, Mumbai and Delhi
cover.cap: About 15 people when I joined, and [about 300 by July 2026](https://manifest-media.in/special-feature/170726/spotlighting-indias-independent-companies-wldd.html).

body: I joined WLDD in Bangalore in January 2023, when the whole company fit on the top floor of one building. There were about fifteen of us, and I was one of the first people in that office. I started as a junior brand strategist. Two months later I was a creative strategist, working on campaigns for brands I had grown up with.

WLDD's edge was meme marketing: funny, quirky, shareable copy that people passed on because it was good, not because it was an ad. We did it for Zomato, Swiggy One, Zepto and Bingo! Mad Angles. For films, an organic meme push could put people in seats, and the audience never knew the joke they were sharing had been planned.

The engine was distribution. WLDD worked with hundreds of India's biggest meme pages, so one idea could land everywhere on the same day. Releases for Prime Video, Netflix India, ZEE5, Sony Pictures, Sony Music and South Indian cinema all ran through that network. By [afaqs' count](https://www.afaqs.com/news/mktg/meme-experts-the-new-specialist-agencies-on-the-block), the agency has worked with more than 120 brands on over 1,050 campaigns, with a community of more than 10,000 creators.

I pitched and closed Sony Pictures as WLDD's first international client. [Our Pope's Exorcist cinema stunt](/work/the-popes-exorcist/) was covered by Hindustan Times, India Today and The Indian Express.
I worked on [Thank You Durex](/work/thank-you-durex/), a fan page we built for Durex India. One reel passed 20.9 million views, and I'm the last person in it.
I ran [WLDD's own Instagram](/work/wldd-instagram/). A typical reel went from about 4,000 views to about 19,000.
I worked on ZEE5's Taj: Divided by Blood, Tu Jhoothi Main Makkaar and Kannada cinema, including PR and marketing around Yash and KGF: Chapter 2.

WLDD wali Holi reel by the WLDD team, posted by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil on the agency's Instagram: the whole office covered in Holi colours by the pool

body: Every few months we needed more room. We took the second floor, then the first, then the whole building. Then came a second building, for LIT School.

I left in 2024, at the peak of my time there, to study filmmaking in New York. WLDD kept growing. In February 2025 it [bought ScoopWhoop from The Good Glamm Group](https://www.exchange4media.com/marketing-news/the-good-glamm-group-sells-scoopwhoop-to-wldd-in-rs-20-cr-deal-141145.html) in a deal reported at Rs 20 crore. A month later it [took a majority stake in the sneaker brand 7-10](https://inc42.com/?p=505650), and in June 2025 it [acquired the creative studio Imagined](https://inc42.com/buzz/wldd-acquires-creative-studio-imagined).

By July 2026 it had [about 300 people across Bengaluru, Mumbai and Delhi](https://manifest-media.in/special-feature/170726/spotlighting-indias-independent-companies-wldd.html). In September 2026, [Adfactors PR and Vikas Khemani bought a stake](https://www.exchange4media.com/pr-and-corporate-communication-news/wldd-secures-strategic-investment-from-adfactors-pr-vikas-khemani-157867.html), and Adfactors PR's CEO joined the board.

That floor taught me three things I still use at [Thava Studio](https://www.instagram.com/thava.studio) in New York. Write it so people want to send it to a friend. Put it where the audience already is, not where you wish they were. And ship it while people are still talking about the thing it's about.
Fifteen desks on a top floor became a company of about 300 people that owns ScoopWhoop. I'm glad I was there when it was small enough that every idea I pitched might get made.
When a team is small enough that every idea can ship, speed and taste beat budget.

title: What the Pope's Exorcist taught me about virality.
dek: And why most brands get it wrong.
body: In early 2023, I was a Creative Strategist at WLDD, a scrappy startup of fifteen people sharing one office in Bangalore, India. We had big clients, bigger ambitions, and the kind of energy that only exists when a company is small enough that every idea you pitch might actually get made.

Sony Pictures India came to us with a brief for The Pope's Exorcist, a Hollywood horror film starring Russell Crowe, releasing in Indian theatres. The ask was straightforward: generate buzz, drive awareness, get people talking.

What happened next was covered by [Hindustan Times](https://www.hindustantimes.com/trending/woman-scares-people-in-theatre-as-the-pope-s-exorcist-trailer-plays-on-screen-101680956103411.html) and [The Indian Express](https://indianexpress.com/article/trending/trending-in-india/possessed-woman-growls-at-moviegoers-as-the-popes-exorcist-trailer-plays-in-theatre-8545834/), reached millions of people across India, and earned WLDD its first international Hollywood client. WLDD has since grown from fifteen people to about 300, bought [ScoopWhoop](/work/fifteen-people-on-one-floor/), and become one of India's best-known meme marketing agencies.

I'm not telling you this to brag. I'm telling you this because everything I learned about virality, real virality and not the manufactured kind, I learned from that campaign. And most of it runs counter to what brands are told to do.
1. Virality is not about the brand. It's about the moment.

The biggest mistake I see brands make is putting themselves at the centre of everything they create. Their logo, their tagline, their product shot, front and centre, every single time. The audience doesn't care. The audience cares about themselves, their culture, their emotions, and what's happening in their world right now.

The Pope's Exorcist campaign worked because we didn't lead with the film. We led with the audience's experience of watching a horror trailer in a theatre: the anticipation, the darkness, the collective held breath of a crowd that's about to be scared. We understood that moment viscerally. And we built an idea that hijacked it in a way that felt completely organic.
When people shared the content, they weren't sharing a movie promotion. They were sharing something that made them feel something. That's the difference.
2. Cultural fluency beats production value every single time.

We didn't have a massive budget. We didn't have a celebrity. We didn't have a production crew or a fancy shoot. What we had was a deep understanding of how Indian audiences engage with horror, with cinema, with meme culture, and with the specific pleasure of being scared in a crowded theatre with strangers.

That cultural fluency, knowing what would make this specific audience stop scrolling, lean in and send it to their friends, was worth more than any production budget. I grew up watching films the way Indian audiences watch films: loudly, communally, emotionally. I knew what would land because I was the audience.

This is why I'm always sceptical of global brands that create one piece of content and try to push it across every market. Virality is local before it's global. It spreads because it feels like it was made for you specifically, not for everyone vaguely.
3. The idea has to be willing to be uncomfortable.

Safe content does not go viral. I have never seen a perfectly polished, brand-approved, legal-reviewed, twelve-rounds-of-feedback piece of content genuinely break through. Not once. The content that travels is always the content that made someone in the approval chain a little bit nervous.

The Pope's Exorcist campaign had an edge to it. It was bold. It made people do a double-take. It wasn't the kind of content a large agency with a lot to lose would have approved in the first round. But WLDD was fifteen people with everything to gain and very little to protect, and that freedom was the creative advantage.
If every idea gets smoothed down until it's inoffensive and forgettable, you are not making content. You're making wallpaper. And nobody shares wallpaper.
4. Memes are not a tactic. They are a language.

At WLDD, meme marketing was at the core of how we thought about everything. Not because memes are "trendy", but because memes are how large portions of the internet actually communicate. They are cultural shorthand. They travel fast because they carry meaning efficiently, and they're participatory by nature: people remix them, respond to them, and pass them on.

The brands that treat memes as a tactic ("let's do a meme this week") almost always get it wrong. It feels forced because it is. The brands that understand meme culture as a living, breathing language, and speak it fluently and in real time, are the ones whose content actually gets shared by real people to other real people.

The Pope's Exorcist campaign spoke that language. It didn't just use a meme format. It understood the emotional grammar of how Indian internet culture reacts to horror, to cinema, to the unexpected. That's the difference between speaking a language and just knowing a few words.

The internet moves fast. Cultural moments have a half-life measured in hours, sometimes minutes. One of the biggest advantages of being at a small, scrappy startup like early WLDD was that we could go from idea to execution in a fraction of the time a larger organisation would need. We could see a moment happening, make something about it, and be live before anyone else had finished their first internal approval email.

This is a structural problem for large brands, not a creative one. The people with the best ideas are usually close to the culture. They're young, they're online, they feel the moment in real time. But those people are often several layers away from anyone who can say yes fast enough for the moment to still be alive. By the time the idea gets approved, the moment has passed.

If you're building a brand or running a marketing team, the most valuable thing you can do is create a short approval path for real-time content. Trust the people who are closest to the culture. Give them room to move quickly. A good idea published in time beats a perfect idea published too late, every single time.

Virality is not a formula. It's not a checklist. It's not a budget line item. It's what happens when the right idea meets the right audience at the right moment, and someone was brave enough to make it without waiting for permission.

The campaign changed WLDD's trajectory. It changed mine too. It confirmed something I had always believed: that the principles of great filmmaking and the principles of great marketing are the same. Know your audience. Build to an emotion. Be specific. Be brave. Move fast.

I eventually left WLDD, at the peak of my time there, which I'd recommend to anyone, to pursue filmmaking full time in New York. I made the Dean's List at the New York Film Academy, shot [Love Is Stronger Than Hate](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VQRsfpHgC38) as director of photography (it won Best Costume Design at the Follow Your Heart Film Festival), and founded [Thava Studio](https://www.instagram.com/thava.studio), a creative studio working with brands across New York, Los Angeles, Philadelphia and Bangalore.

Everything I build now, whether it's a social media strategy for a restaurant in Brooklyn, a short film shot on New York rooftops, or a content system for a luxury brand, runs on the same instincts I developed in that first WLDD office. The audience is always the film. The brand is always the character. The moment is always the script.

If you're building something right now and trying to figure out how to make it travel, stop asking how to go viral. Start asking what your audience actually feels, what cultural moment you're speaking into, and whether you're brave enough to say something worth sharing. The rest tends to follow.

title: Why I broke the 180-degree rule.
dek: One cell, one light, and a camera that switches sides when the power does.

cover.alt: Agent X, an interrogation scene directed by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil: Dillon Cain as the agent leans across a table toward Nathan Flores as the seated prisoner, under a single overhead light
cover.cap: Agent X. With Dillon Cain and Nathan Flores. Director of photography Yoey Garfield.

body: At the New York Film Academy, the production workshop is where you get a real studio, a crew and a dolly, and one scene to prove you can run a set. I built a prison cell.

The scene is Agent X. An agent visits a prisoner serving a life sentence and makes him an offer. The film around it was never shot, so here's the subtext: the offer is a second chance, if the prisoner signs his life over and works for the agent as a hitman. He'd be paid. He might die in the field. Either way, he'd be out.
Agent X, an interrogation scene directed by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil, with Dillon Cain and Nathan Flores

We built the set inside the studio to look like a cell: one room, one table, lit from a single light above, with another light picking out the actors' heads. Faces fall in and out of shadow every time someone leans in. We laid dolly track on both sides of the table, so the camera could move with whoever held the power.
Yoey Garfield shot it on a RED Komodo. Dillon Cain and Nathan Flores played the two men.
The power is in the blocking

At the start, the agent stands and leans over the table while the prisoner sits. He's the one asking, so he's the one dominating. The prisoner keeps saying no. He's already rotting in there for life, so what could the agent possibly do for him?

The agent slides a granola bar across the table. By the midpoint the prisoner takes it and eats it. That's the first crack: he's starting to see that this offer is the only second chance he'll ever get.

Film school teaches the 180-degree rule early. Draw an imaginary line between two characters and keep the camera on one side of it, so the audience never loses track of who's where. Cross it, and the cut feels wrong.

That's exactly why I crossed it. For most of the scene the camera stays on one side of the line, while the agent is in control. The moment the prisoner is convinced, the power flips, and so does the camera. You should feel something change before anyone says it out loud.
Nobody in my class understood the choice, and my professors didn't agree with it either. I shot it anyway. The rule exists to keep the audience settled, and at that moment I wanted them unsettled.
The camera crosses the line at the exact moment he does.
Crew: assistant director Yi Chan (Ethan), gaffer Yamira, grip Nicolas, sound Cito, first AC Jeff, second AC Ramon. More of my films are in the [short films section](/#films).

title: Hub, hype and hygiene.
dek: The posting mix behind every brand I've run.

cover.alt: Hub, hype and hygiene, the content mix used by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil: hub about half to 60% of posts, hype around 30%, hygiene 10 to 20%
cover.cap: The mix I start every account with. It moves with the brand.

body: Every brand I've run gets the same posting plan, from film and FMCG campaigns at WLDD in Bangalore to cafes in New York. I call it hub, hype and hygiene.

I didn't invent the shape. Google's YouTube playbook for brands split content into hero, hub and hygiene, later renamed [hero, hub and help](https://thinkwithgoogle.com/marketing-strategies/video/build-a-content-plan). What I changed is the third H. Hero content is the big tentpole moment, and most brands I work with can't afford one every month. Trends, though, show up every week for free. So my third H is hype.
Hub: what you do, in your own world

Hub is the everyday posting: what the brand makes, what happens inside it, and the people who run it. For a cafe that's the menu, the space and the regulars. For a gym it's the workouts. It also covers anything shot in the brand's own surroundings, so a skit where the waiter plays a character is still hub, because it lives where the brand lives.

Hygiene keeps the mission visible. If a restaurant's promise is authentic Indian food, or authentic halal food, hygiene posts explain it: where the flavours come from, how a dish is made, what makes it the real thing. They're often simple, information-first posts or a talking head, and they're the posts people check before they decide to trust you.
Hype: the trend, moved into your world
Hype is whatever is trending that week, a sound, a pop culture moment, a dance, rebuilt inside the brand's own setting. It's the fastest way to reach people who don't follow you yet.
Hub: about half to 60% of posts
Hygiene: 10 to 20%, depending on the brand

The mix matters more than any single post. Post only hype and you run out of trends, and the audience forgets what you sell. I've seen a pet food brand whose page is all office trends, so people think it's an office company. Post only hub and nobody new finds you. Post only hygiene and it reads like a brochure. With a mix, you can post every day without the page getting saturated.

Everywhere: film and OTT launches, FMCG, food and retail pages at WLDD, influencer pages and PR for actors, and through Thava Studio in America, cafes, restaurants and real estate. Three of the case studies show it working:
[Fetchy](/work/fetchy/): the plan took YouTube Shorts from 600 to 1,000 views each to above 2,000, and one Short passed 616,000.
[Infamous Coconuts](/work/infamous-coconuts/): we rebuilt the feed around hub, hype and hygiene, and the typical reel went from about 5,000 views to 98,000.
[Thank You Durex](/work/thank-you-durex/): memes as hooks, with skits and trends built around the product. One reel passed 20.9 million views.

Two studies back up why hype stays at about 30% and not 100%. A 2023 study in the Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing found that brand memes build the relationship when they're easy to get, feel new and fit the brand, and that sarcasm works against them ([read the study](https://emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/JRIM-01-2023-0029/full/html)). Another, in the Journal of Consumer Marketing, found that meme posts read as funnier and earn more likes and shares, but lower engagement on cause-related campaigns ([read the study](https://www.emerald.com/jcm/article/doi/10.1108/JCM-09-2024-7221/1253616/Brand-posts-with-memes-on-social-media-perceived)). Humour travels, but it has to fit the brand and the moment.
If you post one kind of thing every day, the page gets saturated. Mix the three and you can keep posting.

title: How we plan a micro drama in a day.
dek: The AI production stack behind 12+ series.
short: Micro dramas, planned in a day

cover.alt: Close-up of an actress on a phone call in warm light, from Demo Day, a Canvas series directed by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil, produced by Abhinav Singla, shot by Kais Vasaya
cover.cap: Still from [Demo Day](/series/demo-day/), a 10-episode Canvas series shot at Harvard in under four days.

body: We've planned shoots the night before and rolled camera the next morning. Cast confirmed, locations locked, call sheet out. Nobody panicked.

That isn't a flex about speed. It's the only way a micro drama works on a startup budget. This year I directed [12+ short-form series](/#series) for [Canvas](https://creatorsarethenewstudios.com/), a New York and Mumbai micro drama studio, shot across New York, Boston, Baltimore, San Francisco and Los Angeles. Most were shot in three or four days.
The short version: we plan in Directure AI, we finish in a Claude Code pipeline, and every shoot doubles as ad creative. Here's how each piece works, and what I've learned running it.
Why micro dramas need a different production model
A micro drama episode runs under two minutes. A season is five to ten episodes. The budget is a fraction of a short film's, and the shoot is three or four days.
You can't spend a week in pre-production on a series that shoots in three days. The planning has to move as fast as the shoot.

There's a second constraint. Every Canvas series is creator-led: a creator with a real audience is attached from day one, like Ruhani Sharma (1.4M followers) on [Dear NYC](/series/dear-nyc/) or Robert Maxwell (1.1M) on [Red Flags](/series/red-flags/). Their calendar is the production calendar. When it moves, everything moves.
Step 1: Plan everything in Directure AI
We plan most of our series in [Directure AI](https://directureai.com/), a production planning platform built in New York by Abhinav Singla and his team.

You upload the script and it breaks it down: characters, locations, props, wardrobe and scene requirements. AI Boarding turns scenes into shot cards and suggests how each shot should be made. From there you build shoot days, call sheets and a budget, all connected to the same script.

The real win isn't the breakdown. It's what happens when the script changes. You see right away what a rewrite does to the schedule and the budget, so we rewrite for logistics, not just story. If two scenes can share a location, they do. If a scene needs a fourth shoot day, it gets cut or moved.

[Demo Day](/series/demo-day/): 10 episodes at Harvard and around Boston in under four days. On the morning we left New York, our lead actor had to drop out. We recast that morning, rewrote the role in the car on the drive up, and wrote each day's episodes around what we'd already shot. [Here's the full story of that shoot](/work/ten-episodes-at-harvard-in-under-four-days/).

[Face Value](/series/face-value/): a four-part micro documentary shot inside New York Fashion Week. The world was already there, so we built no sets and spent nothing on production design. [Watch Face Value on Canvas](https://www.canvasott.com/video/cmw1t94ey00kxs60ek9qkz9gt).
Step 2: A Claude Code pipeline for post-production
Post is where most short-form budgets quietly die. Ten episodes means ten edits, ten sets of graphics, ten rounds of notes.

I run Claude Code with agents connected to Premiere Pro, Higgsfield and ElevenLabs. It handles the repetitive layers: assembling selects, building animations and infographics, generating AI shots where a live shot isn't possible, and temp voice. One series, Made in the Valley, was produced end to end this way.

The tool isn't the advantage. Everyone can buy the same subscription. The advantage is the training. I've spent months teaching my setup our scripts, our edit rules, our hooks and our revision notes as reusable skills. Each production makes it better at the next one.

One rule we don't break: it can't look like AI. You can usually tell when something was made with a default setup, so we feed it as many references as we can, and every output goes through a human edit.
Step 3: Every shoot becomes ad creative
A series isn't finished when it's uploaded. It's finished when people watch it.
So every shoot also produces marketing:
Snippet ads cut from the strongest few seconds of each episode
Organic vox pops and talking heads filmed on the same days
Fast revisions from performance data: which hook held, which didn't, and new cuts built around the winners
Each show is also packaged for its creator's audience, so it travels on Instagram and YouTube as well as the app.
It doesn't choose the story. It doesn't cast the face that makes you stop scrolling. It doesn't know when a take is true.

What it does is buy back time for those decisions. On a three-day shoot, the hours we save in planning and post are the hours we spend on performance, on the hook, and on the cliffhanger that sells the next episode.
Speed also exposes weak scripts faster. When you can plan a shoot in a day, there's nowhere for a bad idea to hide.

Your turn: what's the one part of production you'd hand to AI first, and the one part you'd never hand over? [Tell me in the comments on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/how-we-plan-micro-drama-day-ai-production-stack-12-thavarayil-zkpte/). I read every comment.

title: Ten episodes at Harvard in under four days.
dek: And no lead actor on the morning we left.

cover.alt: Night still from Demo Day, directed by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil: an actress leans on a bridge railing with city lights behind her
cover.cap: Still from [Demo Day](/series/demo-day/). Director of photography Kais Vasaya.

body: In August we shot a 10-episode web series at Harvard in under four days, and it turned into one of the wildest shoots I've been part of.

It started with Abhinav Singla, owner of [Directure AI](https://directureai.com/), getting a pitch slot at Harvard. He asked if we could turn the whole trip into something more. We said yes before we had a script. The idea was two roommate founders building an AI-powered filmmaking tool, pitching it to investors, and the real Harvard pitch would become the final episode of the series.
We had a baseline idea and three days to shoot it.
The morning we were supposed to leave

Our lead actor stopped answering his phone. We called for hours with nothing back. We pushed our 9am pitch to the afternoon and started driving anyway, hoping he'd still show up. He did, for about twenty minutes, before telling us he had a family emergency and had to turn around and go home.
So now we had no actor, no backup, four hours from New York, and ten episodes still to shoot.

I called every actor I knew in the city. Nobody could clear four days on a few hours' notice. Abhinav ended up calling someone he'd only met once, at a workshop months earlier. Her name is Chewie. She picked up, heard the pitch, and said yes without hesitating for a second. We rewrote her entire role in the car on the drive up.
We missed the actual pitch. We ended up faking it in an empty auditorium the next day, just to get the footage we needed.
What followed was four days of 17-hour shoots, sleeping two hours at a time, and writing each episode based on what we'd already shot the day before, because there was never time to write it first.

Everyone did a bit of everything. Abhinav was acting and producing, Kais Vasaya was shooting as director of photography, and at different points all of us were writing, art directing, or just throwing out ideas because that's what the day needed.
Ten episodes, no real plan, and honestly one of the best things I've made this year.

This is the shoot I think about when people ask how we plan a series so fast. [Here's the system we use now](/work/how-we-plan-a-micro-drama-in-a-day/), and [here's the series page for Demo Day](/series/demo-day/).

title: We just closed a $10,000 client for Growvior.
dek: The only sales strategy I've ever used, and it costs nothing.
short: The only sales strategy I use

cover.alt: Growvior services graphic: custom software, creative media and branding, website development and mobile apps, from the company co-founded by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil and Agrajh Ak
cover.cap: Growvior, the software company I co-founded with Agrajh Ak.

body: I didn't cold email a database. I didn't run ads. I didn't have a sales deck. I just talked to people.

My co-founder [Agrajh Ak](https://www.linkedin.com/in/agrajh-ak/) and I just signed our biggest client to date at [Growvior](https://www.instagram.com/growvior/): a $10,000 engagement with a New York-based tech startup that is building something genuinely exciting in the South Asian and Asian community here in America. They are founding-stage. They came to us because they needed a software partner who understood their vision from day one.

I'm not going to tell you the client details. That's their story to tell when they're ready. What I am going to tell you is exactly how we got here. Because it has nothing to do with cold outreach funnels, LinkedIn automation tools, or any growth hack you've read about in a newsletter.
It has everything to do with one thing: talking to people.
Stop waiting for someone to ask. Just tell them what you do.

I run two companies. [Thava Studio](https://www.instagram.com/thava.studio/), a creative agency handling social media strategy, content production and brand direction for clients across New York, Los Angeles, Philadelphia and Bangalore. And Growvior, an AI-integrated software company building products for clients in New York and India. I'm also a filmmaker. My work spans restaurants in Brooklyn, vocal coaches, realtors, EdTech platforms, fashion model PR, a film production house and now a founding-stage tech startup.
When I tell people this, the most common reaction is: "Wait, you do all of that?"
Yes. And I never hide any of it. Because you never know which part of what you do is the exact thing someone in the room has been looking for.

Maybe the real estate agent you meet at a dinner needs a website. Maybe the DJ you bump into at a film screening has no idea how to grow his Instagram. Maybe the cafe owner you chat with at a coffee shop has been trying to figure out how to make reels that actually get views. Maybe the app founder in your network has built something great but has no social media strategy to get it to market. Maybe the graphic designer you follow online needs someone to handle their email marketing and client proposals.

All of these people exist. I have found every single one of them, not through a CRM, not through paid ads, but through genuine conversation. Through asking questions, listening properly, and then saying: "Actually, that's something I can help with."
The chain reaction nobody talks about.

Since I started my company in New York, I have brought in 10+ clients entirely through conversation and referral. Not one of them came from a cold database. Every single one came from a chain that started with one person (someone from a film set, a wedding I attended, a real estate contact, a graphic designer I collaborated with once) who knew what I did and connected me to someone who needed it.

This is how it works in practice. You meet someone. You tell them about your work, all of it, not just the part that seems relevant to them in that moment. You ask about their work. You listen. Somewhere in that conversation, a connection forms. Maybe they don't need you right now. But they know someone who does. And they remember you because you were specific, you were genuine, and you weren't trying to close them. You were just talking to them like a human being.

Then they make an introduction. And that introduction leads to a conversation. And that conversation leads to a client. And that client leads to a referral. That's the chain. It's not a funnel. It's not a system. It's just what happens when you talk to people consistently and honestly about what you do.
Nobody is sitting in a room judging you for talking about your work. Nobody. The only person who thinks it's too much is you.
Pitch everything. You never know what lands.

I used to wonder if talking about all the different things I do made me look unfocused. I don't wonder that anymore. The breadth is the advantage. Because in any given conversation, I might be useful as a filmmaker, as a social media strategist, as a web developer, as a software co-founder, or as a creative director. The more surface area you show, the more likely something connects.

When I met the team behind our newest $10K client, the conversation started in a completely different context. It wasn't a sales meeting. It was just a conversation between people who were building things in New York. But I talked about Growvior. I talked about what we build, who we build it for, and what problems we solve. And it turned out they had been looking for exactly that: a software partner who could move fast, understood their community, and was genuinely invested in what they were building.
That's it. That's the whole strategy.
Your internet presence is your silent pitch. Make it work for you.

Here's something people underestimate: even when you're not in a room with someone, your online presence is pitching on your behalf. Every time a potential client searches your name, visits your Instagram, or reads an article you've written, they're deciding whether to trust you before they've even said hello.

If you don't have a strong portfolio yet, build toward it, not away from it. Show something close to what they need. Show your thinking, your process, your taste. Confidence in the conversation means nothing if there's nothing to back it up when they Google you at midnight before deciding to reply.

And if you genuinely don't have the experience yet, be honest about it and be confident anyway. Every single thing you have done was the first time you did it. The client doesn't need you to have done it a hundred times. They need you to understand their problem and believe you can solve it. Those are two different things, and only one of them requires experience.
Take the first step. Make the mistake. Do it bigger next time.

I have made mistakes with clients. I have underpriced work, overpromised timelines, and taken on projects I had to figure out in real time. Every single one of those experiences made me better: at the work, at the pricing, at the conversation, at understanding what I can and cannot deliver. You don't learn any of that by waiting until you're ready. You only learn it by starting.

The $10,000 client didn't happen because I had everything figured out. It happened because I had been building, talking, learning, and showing up consistently for long enough that when the right conversation happened, I was ready for it.
You are closer than you think. Talk to the person next to you. Tell them everything you do. Ask them what they're building. Listen. And then ask if they know anyone who might need what you have.

title: Your product doesn't need an ad. It needs a format.
dek: What a famous curry taught me about creators with no budget.

cover.alt: Brick Lane Curry House case by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil: 1.47M views on one phaal reel, with zero paid creators
cover.cap: From the [Brick Lane Curry House case study](/work/brick-lane-phaal/).

body: Brick Lane Curry House has a dish with a reputation. Its phaal is the curry Adam Richman took on in Man v. Food, and people still walk in asking for it by name. That's the kind of story most brands would pay for. What the restaurant didn't have was a budget for paid creators.
So we stopped treating the phaal like a menu item and started treating it like a format.

The phaal started as the least interesting dish on the menu. Chef Satinder Sharma, who opened Brick Lane on East 6th Street in 2002, decided that if he was going to make something spicy, he'd do it justice. Habaneros first, then Scotch bonnets, bhut jolokia and the Carolina Reaper, bought straight from Ed Currie, the grower who bred it.

When Man v. Food showed up, the dish "snowballed into something so big, unintentionally," he told me. He calls it the infamous phaal who made them famous. A story like that is already doing the work an ad would do. It just needs somewhere to happen every week.
A challenge is already a show

Look at what the phaal challenge already has: a known villain, a clear stake and a reaction at the end. That isn't an ad. It's a show that can run every week. Formats are what bring people back, because the audience knows the shape and wants to see who's next.

So we turned the challenge into a recurring content property on the restaurant's own channels. One phaal reel, a collaboration with [First We Feast](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DDfpOyOvk33/), reached 1.47 million views.

A format also fixes the budget problem. If the phaal is a show, creators aren't people you pay to hold your food up to the camera. They're contestants, and they want the content as much as the restaurant wants the reach.

I pitched more than ten food creators myself, DMs and all, on a zero-budget creator strategy. We brought in Priya's Plates as our guest and posted [her attempt](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DBWjEWBvpIV/) as a collaboration, so it reached both audiences at once. It passed 58,000 views with nearly 300 shares.

Most brands already have one and walk past it. Look for the thing customers repeat about you without being asked: the dish people dare each other to order, the question every new client asks, the ritual your regulars have.

Then give it a shape that repeats. The same setup, the same stakes, a new face every time. Run it on your own channels so you own it, and invite creators in as guests so their audiences meet you inside a story instead of an ad break.
If your product has a famous story, it doesn't need an ad. It needs a format.
